clinicalPearls: A rare, locally aggressive malignant bone tumour arising from notochordal remnants along the midline axial skeleton
Characteristically involves the clivus/skull base, the mobile spine, and the sacrococcygeal region, the last being the commonest site
Presentation is often insidious: sacral tumours cause low back or perineal pain and bowel or bladder dysfunction, while clival tumours cause headache, diplopia, and other cranial nerve palsies
Histology shows physaliphorous (bubbly, vacuolated) cells in a myxoid matrix, and the tumour expresses brachyury (TBXT), a highly specific nuclear marker
Brachyury immunohistochemistry distinguishes chordoma from morphological mimics such as chondrosarcoma and metastatic carcinoma
En bloc surgical resection with clear margins offers the best chance of control, but midline skull base and sacral locations make complete excision technically demanding
High-dose specialised radiotherapy, including particle (proton) therapy, is frequently used adjuvantly or when complete resection is not achievable
Local recurrence is common and metastasis can occur late, so prolonged surveillance is required
reference.pathophysiology: Chordoma arises from remnants of the embryonic notochord that persist within the midline axial skeleton. The transcription factor brachyury (encoded by TBXT), essential for notochord development, is characteristically overexpressed and is central to tumour cell survival and phenotype, providing both a diagnostic marker and a therapeutic target of interest. Germline duplication of the TBXT locus underlies rare familial chordoma. The tumour grows slowly but invades bone and adjacent neural and soft-tissue structures, and its deep midline location, proximity to critical neurovascular structures, and tendency to seed along surgical tracts make wide resection difficult and local recurrence frequent.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic carcinoma to the axial skeleton
Giant cell tumour of the sacrum
Ecchordosis physaliphora and benign notochordal cell tumour
Meningioma or other skull base tumours (for clival lesions)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the axial site to define soft-tissue and neural extent and relation to critical structures
CT to assess bony destruction and matrix and to plan surgery
Dedicated skull base or spinal imaging for surgical and radiotherapy planning
Chest CT and whole-body imaging for staging given the potential for late metastasis
Biopsy with careful tract planning to avoid seeding, ideally coordinated with the resecting surgeon
Immunohistochemistry including brachyury (TBXT), cytokeratins, and S100 to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Progressive cranial nerve palsies, diplopia, or headache from a clival mass
New bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle anaesthesia, or perineal pain from a sacral tumour
A destructive midline axial bone lesion with a soft-tissue component
Recurrence along a previous biopsy or surgical tract
Late development of pulmonary or other distant metastases
reference.prognosis: Chordoma is a slow-growing but relentlessly recurring tumour; long-term outcome depends chiefly on achieving complete en bloc resection and on tumour location, with incompletely resected skull base and sacral tumours prone to repeated recurrence and eventual metastasis in a proportion of patients.
pitfalls: Confusing chordoma with chondrosarcoma without brachyury immunohistochemistry, which has major treatment implications
Performing an ill-planned biopsy that seeds tumour along the tract and compromises curative resection
Underestimating the extent of neural and soft-tissue involvement on inadequate imaging
Settling for intralesional or piecemeal excision when en bloc resection is feasible
Discontinuing surveillance too early, missing late local recurrence or distant metastasis
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Treatment is built around maximal safe surgical resection plus adjuvant radiotherapy, since wide-margin gross total resection is often not achievable, especially at the skull base
There are no validated prognostic factors for recurrence, so most patients need a prolonged surgical/radiotherapy course followed by long-term surveillance rather than fixed lines of therapy

Immunohistochemistry helps distinguish chordoma (keratin and epithelial membrane antigen positive) from chondrosarcoma (S100 positive, keratin negative), which matters because chondrosarcoma has a more favorable outcome

For low-grade skull base chondrosarcoma, deferring immediate postoperative radiotherapy in favor of MRI surveillance after maximal safe resection is a reasonable strategy given comparable long-term disease-free survival with salvage treatment

Surgery is the backbone of care, providing diagnostic tissue and reducing tumor bulk to improve subsequent radiotherapy; complete resection is the goal when achievable, typically via combined neurosurgical and otolaryngology teams
Adjuvant radiotherapy after resection is a mainstay given the frequent inability to achieve negative margins, and can serve as primary treatment when surgery is not possible
Particle beam radiotherapy (proton or carbon-ion) is regarded as the most effective modality for skull base and spinal chordoma, allowing higher doses while sparing adjacent critical structures
Stereotactic radiosurgery is an option for small-volume residual or recurrent disease as adjuvant or salvage treatment

Systemic therapy is reserved for advanced, recurrent, or metastatic chordoma rather than routine primary management; a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib has shown disease control benefit, with an mTOR inhibitor added for those who progress
A mutant-IDH1 inhibitor has shown benefit specifically in IDH1-mutant chondrosarcoma, not chordoma
PARP inhibition and immune checkpoint inhibition are being explored investigationally in advanced chordoma but remain under clinical trial evaluation rather than established practice
There is no established standard cytotoxic chemotherapy regimen for chordoma

Long-term surveillance with cross-sectional imaging of the primary site plus a baseline chest x-ray is recommended, with baseline endocrine and neuro-ophthalmologic evaluation for skull base tumors when relevant

Chordoma and chondrosarcoma should be managed by a specialist multidisciplinary team from diagnosis, with early referral to centers offering particle beam radiotherapy or sarcoma/neuro-oncology trial access for advanced disease
